--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án B – 5.30 (5 giờ rưỡi).
• Vì sao đúng: Jane chốt "Half past five! I finish at five, fifteen minutes to get there, fifteen minutes for coffee in the courtyard first" và kết lại "Five thirty, gallery steps".
• 4.00 sai: là kế hoạch trước khi đổi ca "Four was the plan before my shift changed — I'm at the clinic until five now, no escape".
• 6.00 sai: quá sát giờ tour "Six cuts it fine, though — the guided tour starts at six and we'd miss the introduction rushing in".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi GẶP LÚC MẤY GIỜ, đáp án có thể là mốc "rưỡi" nằm GIỮA hai mốc chẵn đã nêu. Đừng chỉ nghe số giờ — nghe cả "half past", "quarter to" và câu nhắc lại ở cuối.

question_text: Lalia is talking to her friend about her upcoming trip. How much does she think the bus fare will be?
explanation:
W: Three days until my trip! I'm budgeting every penny tonight.
M: Very organised, Lalia! What's left to figure out?
W: The bus fare to the coast, mainly. My cousin took that route last year and paid four fifty.
M: Four pounds fifty? That was the summer festival price — they double everything in festival week.
W: That's what I hoped! The website mentions three pounds for peak times...
M: Peak is weekday mornings, but you're travelling Saturday afternoon, aren't you?
W: Exactly — off-peak. So with my student card on top... I think the fare will be two pounds fifty. Two fifty, I'm almost sure.
M: Two fifty sounds right for off-peak with the discount. Budget three, to be safe!
W: Two fifty in the plan, three in the pocket. See — THIS is why I budget with a friend!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án A – £2.5 (hai bảng rưỡi).
• Vì sao đúng: Lalia tự tính ra "So with my student card on top... I think the fare will be two pounds fifty. Two fifty, I'm almost sure" và bạn cô xác nhận "Two fifty sounds right for off-peak with the discount".
• £4.5 sai: là giá người chị họ trả trong tuần lễ hội "That was the summer festival price — they double everything in festival week".
• £3 sai: là giá giờ cao điểm, còn cô đi chiều thứ Bảy "Peak is weekday mornings, but you're travelling Saturday afternoon".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi GIÁ VÉ, ba con số gắn với ba điều kiện khác nhau (mùa lễ hội / giờ cao điểm / off-peak + giảm giá sinh viên). Xác định điều kiện của CHÍNH người nói trước rồi mới chọn số.

question_text: How much can Max pay for the computer?
options: 200 pounds
250 pounds
300 pounds
explanation:
M: So, Max — you said you're finally replacing that ancient laptop. What's the budget?
W: Wait, I heard the good ones start at three hundred pounds. Can you even afford that?
M: Three hundred is the shop price for the new model, yes — completely out of my league right now.
W: What about that refurbished one your cousin offered? Two hundred, wasn't it?
M: It was, but he sold it last week — I was too slow, story of my life.
W: So what CAN you actually spend?
M: I've done the maths this morning: with my savings plus selling the old one, I can pay two hundred and fifty. That's my absolute ceiling — two fifty, not a penny more.
W: Two fifty is workable! The computer fair is on Saturday — you'll find something good for that.
M: Saturday it is. Come with me and stop me from overspending!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án B – 250 pounds.
• Vì sao đúng: "with my savings plus selling the old one, I can pay two hundred and fifty. That's my absolute ceiling — two fifty, not a penny more."
• 200 pounds sai: là giá chiếc máy tân trang của người anh họ nhưng đã bán mất ("he sold it last week").
• 300 pounds sai: là giá máy mới ngoài cửa hàng, vượt khả năng ("completely out of my league right now").
👉 Mẹo: "How much CAN he pay" là hỏi khả năng chi trả, không phải giá niêm yết; bám cụm "I can pay", "my ceiling".

question_text: What do people think about this promotion campaign?
options: It makes exaggerated claims about the product.
It provides too little information about the product.
It focuses too much on the product's low price.
explanation:
Our consumer affairs slot tonight looks at the advertising campaign that everybody seems to be arguing about: the one for the new energy drink, Spark. What do viewers actually think of it? I've read hundreds of comments this week, and a clear pattern has emerged. Nobody is saying the adverts are short of information; if anything, they're crowded with facts and figures about the product. Nor is anyone complaining about a fixation on low prices. The price is barely mentioned at all. What people object to, again and again, is the promises. Drink this, the adverts suggest, and you'll run faster, think sharper and sleep better, all by Thursday. Instead of being won over, viewers become suspicious. One phrase turned up in comment after comment: too good to be true. When your audience starts quoting that old saying back at you, your advertising has achieved the opposite of its purpose.

As for my own professional assessment, the company seems to be worried about the wrong things. Its executives fear the campaign is aimed at the wrong group of customers. My analysis says the targeting is actually rather precise; the young commuters it was designed for are exactly the ones sharing it. They also worry that it hasn't attracted enough public attention, yet everyone I meet has seen these adverts at least once. The real issue is financial. Prime-time television slots, a famous director, three separate filming locations abroad: the bill is enormous. I've run the figures several ways, and even the most hopeful sales forecast won't bring back more than half of what's been spent. In advertising, fame is easy to buy. Profit is the part that requires arithmetic.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: It makes exaggerated claims about the product. Bằng chứng: "What people object to, again and again, is the promises." + "too good to be true". Bẫy: thiếu information bị bác ("crowded with facts and figures"); low price bị bác ("The price is barely mentioned at all").
2. Đáp án: It costs too much to make compared with the possible return. Bằng chứng: "the bill is enormous" + "even the most hopeful sales forecast won't bring back more than half of what's been spent". Bẫy: "wrong group of customers" và "enough public attention" là lo ngại của lãnh đạo, bị phân tích bác bỏ.

question_text: Describe the two pictures.
explanation: The first picture shows a farm with people working outdoors. A man is carrying a basket of vegetables, and a woman is feeding chickens. There are also crops, a red barn, a tractor, some cows and other farm animals. It looks like a peaceful countryside place. The second picture shows a modern office. Some people are working on laptops, while others are talking with colleagues. The office looks bright, busy and professional. Overall, the two pictures show two different working environments: one is natural and physical, while the other is modern and office-based.

extra_data.imageDesc: Ảnh 1: nông trại nắng, người đàn ông áo kẻ đội mũ bê giỏ rau đi phía trước, người phụ nữ đội mũ rơm cho gà ăn bên phải; phía sau là luống rau, hai người làm khác, máy kéo đỏ, kho thóc đỏ và bò. Ảnh 2: văn phòng mở sáng, nhiều người ngồi làm laptop, hai phụ nữ đứng nói chuyện cầm cốc cà phê bên cửa kính lớn.

question_text: Mountain (Version 2)
options: Changing the perspective towards mountain
Unique sense of achievement
Publicity of achievement
The wrong priority
A disturbing revelation
Focus on sustainability

explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
1. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói khái niệm "mountain" đã thay đổi theo thời gian: trước thế kỷ 19 người ta ngại chinh phục, nay công nghệ giúp việc leo núi dễ hơn và núi mang ý nghĩa biểu tượng cho thử thách, phiêu lưu.
2. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nhấn mạnh cảm giác thành tựu rất riêng khi leo núi: vượt qua nỗi sợ, đẩy giới hạn bản thân, và adrenaline tạo cảm giác hưng phấn như các môn thể thao mạo hiểm khác.
3. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói trong thời đại số, thành tích leo núi được chia sẻ rộng rãi trên mạng xã hội, biến cột mốc cá nhân thành sự kiện công khai (public spectacles).
4. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn chỉ ra người leo núi đặt sai thứ tự ưu tiên: quan tâm chụp ảnh cho mạng xã hội hơn là tôn trọng núi, bỏ qua cảnh báo thời tiết và an toàn, dẫn tới tai nạn.
5. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn phơi bày sự thật đáng lo ở Everest: dòng người chen chúc, rác thải và ô nhiễm, thử thách cá nhân biến thành cuộc đua thương mại — tác giả dùng chính từ "disturbing".
6. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn tập trung vào tính bền vững: quy định quản lý rác nghiêm hơn, giới hạn số đoàn leo, các chuyến "clean-up climbs" để dọn rác trên núi.
7. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói trải nghiệm cùng nhau trong môi trường thử thách giúp các cặp đôi hoặc bạn bè gắn bó thân thiết hơn nhờ hỗ trợ và hiểu nhau.

extra_data.title: Mountain (Version 2)

paragraphs.text: The term "mountain" has evolved over time, reflecting not only physical characteristics but also cultural significance. Before the 19th century, people were quite shy when it came to conquering mountains. Today, with the development of technology, reaching the highest peaks has become easier. In contemporary discussions, mountains may symbolize challenges to overcome or destinations for adventure, transcending their geographical attributes.

Climbing a mountain often leads to a profound sense of accomplishment. It represents not just reaching a physical summit but also conquering personal fears and pushing one's limits, creating memories that last a lifetime. Besides, mountain climbing also creates Adrenaline - a hormone that creates a feeling of excitement like when playing other adventure sports.

In today's digital age, sharing achievements has become prevalent. Climbing a mountain is frequently documented on social media, turning personal milestones into public spectacles that inspire others while also raising questions about authenticity.

In recent years, some climbers have become more focused on taking photos for social media than respecting the mountains they visit. Long lines form near popular summits as people wait for the perfect picture, often ignoring weather warnings or safety advice. In some cases, this obsession with online fame has led to serious accidents. It shows how personal image is sometimes valued more than safety or responsibility.

Mount Everest, once a symbol of human courage, has now become a worrying example of how adventure can harm nature. Every climbing season, long lines of climbers crowd the narrow paths to the summit, leaving behind waste and pollution on the fragile slopes. What used to be a personal challenge has turned into a commercial race, where success is measured by photos and fame rather than respect for the mountain. This situation is disturbing because it shows how our desire to conquer the world's highest peak has created serious environmental and moral concerns.

As the number of climbers on Mount Everest continues to rise, the need to focus on sustainability has become urgent. Local authorities and environmental groups are now introducing stricter waste management rules, encouraging climbers to bring back what they carry, and limiting the number of expeditions each season. Some teams have even started "clean-up climbs" to remove rubbish left behind on the slopes. These efforts remind us that protecting the mountain is just as important as reaching its peak. True success on Everest should mean leaving the mountain cleaner and safer for future generations.

Shared experiences in challenging environments, like mountains, can deepen intimacy in relationships. Couples or friends who navigate the challenges of climbing together often find their bonds strengthened through mutual support and understanding.

question_text: What do these two famous writers have in common?
options: They both wrote in the same genre
They both were born in the same country
They both make references to each other in their work
explanation:
In this week's literature lecture we look at two writers who changed modern fiction, Clara Holt and Mateo Ruiz, and at what actually connects them, because every year my students guess wrong. They didn't write in the same genre. Holt wrote long family novels; Ruiz wrote short, strange detective stories. They weren't born in the same country either, or even on the same continent. They met only once, at a festival in 1962, and by all accounts the conversation lasted ten minutes. And yet, if you read them side by side, you start to notice things. A minor character in Holt's third novel is a detective with Ruiz's habits, down to his green umbrella. Two years later, a Ruiz story opens with a line taken almost word for word from Holt. For thirty years they kept up this quiet conversation through their books, nodding to one another across an ocean, and neither of them ever mentioned it in an interview.
What makes them special as artists, though, is something else. Students often describe their style as simple, because the sentences are short. That's misleading. The books are built like puzzles, with timelines that jump and narrators who change halfway through. And when you reach the last page, you're often left unsure what you've just read. Is Holt's famous final chapter a happy ending or a tragic one? Critics have argued about it for fifty years. Did the detective in Ruiz's best-known story solve the crime, or commit it? Ruiz refused to say. Some readers assume the plots come from real events in the writers' lives, but there's very little evidence for that. Their books ask you to do the work yourself, and they rarely hand you a final answer.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: They both make references to each other in their work. Bằng chứng: "A minor character in Holt's third novel is a detective with Ruiz's habits" + "nodding to one another across an ocean". Bẫy: cùng thể loại và cùng quốc gia đều bị phủ nhận ("They didn't write in the same genre"; "They weren't born in the same country either").
2. Đáp án: The meaning of their work is not always easily identified. Bằng chứng: "you're often left unsure what you've just read" + "they rarely hand you a final answer." Bẫy: 'simple' là cách sinh viên mô tả, bị bác ("That's misleading"); 'real events' là giả định của một số độc giả ("very little evidence for that").

question_text: What is the speaker's opinion on this script?
options: The characters' backgrounds are not adequately explored
The setting feels too unrealistic
The dialogue is too complex for viewers
explanation:
The producers asked for my honest notes on this script, so here they are. Let me start with what doesn't worry me. The setting is fine. The mountain hotel where the story unfolds feels real and full of atmosphere; I could almost smell the wood smoke. Nor is the dialogue a problem. The lines are clean, and viewers will follow every scene without effort. What worries me is the people. The lead makes an enormous sacrifice in the third act, and yet the script never tells us who she was before page one. Who raised her? What has she lost already? Why is she so afraid of the sea? We're given her job and her haircut, and almost nothing else. Without those roots, her big moment feels like something the plot needs rather than a choice a human being would make. The audience ends up watching her instead of feeling with her, and the same is true of nearly everyone around her.

So why do scripts keep arriving with this same weakness? Look at the business around them. The studios insist their fast production model increases audience engagement significantly. The streaming platforms advertise the creative freedom their writers enjoy. I've worked under both systems, and the reality is almost the reverse. The pressures of today's industry are damaging the writing itself. Deadlines shrink every year, notes from the marketing department chase whatever trend was popular last month, and commercial boxes must be ticked before human ones. Giving a character a believable past takes weeks of quiet thought, and that is exactly what the modern system refuses to pay for. No wonder the people on the page feel hollow.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: The characters' backgrounds are not adequately explored. Bằng chứng: "the script never tells us who she was before page one. Who raised her? What has she lost already?" Bẫy: setting ("The setting is fine") và dialogue ("Nor is the dialogue a problem") được khen, không phải vấn đề.
2. Đáp án: The new industry demands have a negative influence. Bằng chứng: "The pressures of today's industry are damaging the writing itself." Bẫy: "increases audience engagement significantly" là lời studio, "creative freedom" là quảng cáo của platform — "the reality is almost the reverse".

question_text: What should students do when choosing a career?
options: Choose the same career as their friends
Be flexible and open minded
Focus only on the salary offered
explanation:
As a careers adviser, I meet hundreds of final-year students every spring, and the same two traps catch them again and again. The first is friendship. Whole groups come into my office planning to apply for identical jobs at identical firms, because choosing the same career as your friends feels less frightening than deciding alone. The second is the salary line in the advert. Students rank their futures purely by starting pay, as if nothing else about a job mattered. Both roads tend to end in the same place: sitting at a desk three years later, wondering whose life you're living. What I ask of every student is something harder. Keep your options wide. Go to interviews in fields you'd never considered, talk to people whose work sounds strange to you, and be ready to change direction if something unexpected catches your interest. Treat your first job as one step on a long road. Careers reward curiosity far more often than they reward certainty.

Now, a word about applying. There's a lot of nonsense online at the moment. One popular post claims companies now prefer handwritten applications because they feel more personal. Pure fiction: almost everything has been digital for years. Another insists that most jobs no longer require qualifications. Also wrong; your degree is still what gets you into the interview room. What does deserve your attention is the sheer number of people chasing each position. Where ten graduates applied for a role when I started this job, a hundred apply today, and many of them have spent their summers gaining experience. So collect skills, find real work placements, and polish the story only you can tell, because the candidates sitting next to you are doing exactly that.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: Be flexible and open minded. Bằng chứng: "Keep your options wide. Go to interviews in fields you'd never considered" + "be ready to change direction". Bẫy: "the same career as your friends" và "the salary line" là hai cái bẫy sinh viên hay mắc.
2. Đáp án: They are becoming more competitive. Bằng chứng: "Where ten graduates applied for a role when I started this job, a hundred apply today". Bẫy: "prefer handwritten applications" ("Pure fiction") và "no longer require qualifications" ("Also wrong") là tin trên mạng.

explanation: There are several differences between working on a farm and working in an office. On a farm, people usually take care of animals, plant crops, water vegetables and harvest food. In an office, people usually work with computers, documents, meetings and colleagues. The office is more comfortable because it has desks, chairs, air conditioning and the internet. In my opinion, both jobs are difficult but important. Farm work provides food for people, while office work helps businesses and organizations run well.

question_text: What should students do when choosing a career?
options: Choose the same career as their friends
Be flexible and open minded
Focus only on the salary offered
explanation:
Welcome, final-year students. Today let's talk honestly about life after graduation, starting with the biggest decision of all. Every year I watch the same thing happen. Half the class applies to the same three firms because that's where their friends are going, and the other half chase whichever job pays the most in the first year. Neither approach tends to last. The graduates I see doing well five years on are the ones who didn't lock themselves in too early. One of my former students was sure she'd be a lawyer; she ended up at a charity, loved it, and now runs it. Another took a temporary job in logistics just to pay the rent and discovered a talent he never knew he had. So hold your plans loosely. Say yes to the internship that doesn't quite fit, listen to the idea that sounds odd at first, and be prepared to change direction more than once.
Now, a word about applying. Some of you have heard that firms are impressed by a handwritten letter these days. Please don't. Every application goes through an online system now, and a scanned page will simply be ignored. And don't believe anyone who tells you qualifications no longer matter. They matter more than ever, because there are simply more of you. When I graduated, a good degree and a tidy CV would get you an interview. Last year a single graduate post at a local engineering company received over four hundred applications, and most of them had a degree, a placement and a second language. You'll need to prepare harder, apply earlier and show more than the person sitting next to you.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: Be flexible and open minded. Bằng chứng: "So hold your plans loosely" + "be prepared to change direction more than once." Bẫy: chọn theo bạn bè và chạy theo lương là điều sinh viên hay làm, bị gạt ("Neither approach tends to last").
2. Đáp án: They are becoming more competitive. Bằng chứng: "a single graduate post ... received over four hundred applications" + "show more than the person sitting next to you." Bẫy: handwritten bị gạt ("Please don't ... will simply be ignored"); qualifications vẫn quan trọng ("They matter more than ever").

question_text: What will this musician do in the near future?
options: He will probably retire from singing
He plans to release a new album
He wants to collaborate with younger artists
explanation:
Hello and welcome back to Showbiz Tonight. The question every fan is asking this month: what will the grand old man of soul do next? The internet has its theories. A string of young stars have said how much they'd love to collaborate with him, and the fan forums are convinced a new album is being recorded in secret. I hate to spoil the party, but I spoke to him this morning and he was very clear. There's no album and there won't be any duets. Next month's concert in Manchester is billed as his farewell, and he told me that once the curtain comes down, the microphone goes back in its case for good. His voice isn't what it was, he admitted, and he'd rather leave while the applause is still genuine than watch it fade politely.

So how should we remember him? He doesn't regret his choice of profession for a moment; music, he says, was the only life he could have lived. And when I mentioned the famous review claiming he reached his peak too early, he just laughed. His own favourite records came in his fifties. I've followed his career for thirty years, though, and I came away from the interview with a feeling I can't shake. This man had a voice that could have filled stadiums on every continent, and he never quite let it. He cancelled a world tour because he was nervous of flying, he left dozens of songs unrecorded, and he lost almost a decade fighting his record label. He's a legend in this country. With a little more courage, he might have been a legend everywhere.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: He will probably retire from singing. Bằng chứng: "once the curtain comes down, the microphone goes back in its case for good". Bẫy: "collaborate" và "a new album" là đồn đoán của sao trẻ/fan, bị bác bằng "There's no album and there won't be any duets".
2. Đáp án: He could have been more successful. Bằng chứng: "This man had a voice that could have filled stadiums on every continent, and he never quite let it." + "With a little more courage, he might have been a legend everywhere." Bẫy: "doesn't regret his choice of profession"; "reached his peak too early" là bài review cũ, ông "just laughed".

question_text: What attracts readers to this novel?
options: It is different from his earlier works
It is romantic and soft
It is less famous than his earlier works
explanation:
Welcome to tonight's book programme. Our subject is Shadow in the Night, the novel that seems to be in every handbag and on every bedside table this autumn. I run a small bookshop, and I've never seen anything like it. Now, James Parker spent twenty years writing gentle love stories, and when this book was announced, one trade magazine predicted it would end up less famous than his romances, a forgotten experiment. Instead, I can't keep it on the shelves. And the reason customers give me, again and again, is the very thing the doubters feared: it's nothing like anything he's done before. The candlelit dinners and soft romantic endings are gone. In their place we get a missing witness, a frozen harbour town and a detective who trusts nobody. Readers who thought they knew Parker are meeting a stranger, and that surprise is exactly what's pulling them in.

So what should he do next? His new fans write to the publisher begging him to stay with crime. His loyal older readers want him back with the romance that made his name. I understand both groups, but neither is offering him what he really needs. The professional reviews of this book were generous, and they were also honest. They praised the tension, and they pointed out, quite precisely, that the middle chapters drag and two of the characters are paper-thin. Before Parker types a single line of the next novel, he ought to sit down with those reviews and take every comment seriously. That's how a good writer becomes a great one. Whatever shelf the next book ends up on, his readers will follow.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: It is different from his earlier works. Bằng chứng: "it's nothing like anything he's done before" + "that surprise is exactly what's pulling them in". Bẫy: "soft romantic endings are gone"; "less famous" là dự đoán sai của tạp chí ("Instead, I can't keep it on the shelves").
2. Đáp án: He should listen to critics before writing his next work. Bằng chứng: "Before Parker types a single line of the next novel, he ought to sit down with those reviews and take every comment seriously." Bẫy: tiếp tục dòng crime là mong muốn của fan mới, quay về romance là của độc giả cũ — "neither is offering him what he really needs".

question_text: Why is the book so popular?
options: It uses simple language to describe complex ideas
It was endorsed by a famous celebrity
It contains many colorful illustrations
explanation:
Walk into any bookshop this month and you'll see a pyramid of copies of the new biography of the century's greatest physicist. Why has it sold so well? The rumours offer the wrong answers. No, a famous celebrity didn't endorse it on a chat show; the publicity budget was tiny. And no, it isn't full of colourful pictures. Apart from one small photo section, it's plain text from start to finish. The book's popularity rests on a rarer achievement. The author takes the hardest concepts in modern science and explains them in everyday words that a teenager could follow. People who gave up on physics at school suddenly find themselves understanding relativity over breakfast, because every idea arrives wrapped in an ordinary story: a train, a torch, a falling apple. Making difficulty feel easy is the hardest trick in writing, and she manages it on almost every page.

Naturally, success attracts criticism. Interestingly, nobody accuses the book of choosing entertainment over facts. The science has been checked by experts, and it holds up. Nobody calls it too short to be meaningful, either; it runs to nearly six hundred pages. The complaint that keeps coming back is a different one. Eight years ago, the same author wrote a book about the same man, and this one follows it rather closely: the same structure, the same rhythm, several of the same anecdotes in fresher clothes. Loyal fans call that a signature style. Reviewers call it repetition. If you never read her first book, the debate won't trouble you at all. But if you did, expect a strong feeling that you've walked this road before.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: It uses simple language to describe complex ideas. Bằng chứng: "The author takes the hardest concepts in modern science and explains them in everyday words that a teenager could follow." Bẫy: celebrity endorse là tin đồn ("didn't endorse it"); "colourful pictures" bị bác ("plain text from start to finish").
2. Đáp án: It is similar to the previous book about the scientist. Bằng chứng: "Eight years ago, the same author wrote a book about the same man, and this one follows it rather closely". Bẫy: "nobody accuses the book of choosing entertainment over facts"; "Nobody calls it too short to be meaningful".

question_text: Housing space is more important than farming space.
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
M: Have you heard? The council wants to turn the old car park on Bridge Street into vegetable plots for the neighbourhood.
W: I have, and I can't believe it. There are four thousand families on the waiting list for a flat in this town. Surely a roof over somebody's head comes before a row of carrots?
M: I'll grant you there's a shortage, but is it really one or the other? There's land all over town that's been empty for years. Not every square metre has to become a block of flats.
W: Try telling that to my sister. She's been on our sofa since March because she can't find anywhere to rent.
M: That's tough. But I'll be honest, the whole idea excites me. Picking tomatoes on a rooftop, bees in the middle of the high street, neighbours swapping courgettes over the fence. I'd sign up tomorrow.
W: Really? It all sounds a bit twee to me. Muddy knees and slugs aren't my idea of a relaxing Saturday. I'd much rather pay somebody else to do the digging.
M: Each to their own. There's a serious side to it, though. The population here grows every year, and I can't see the supermarkets keeping up for ever. Sooner or later there won't be enough to go round unless we grow more of it ourselves.
W: Oh, come on. The lorries arrive every morning and the shelves are full by eight. When did you last see an empty shelf that wasn't during a snowstorm? The system copes perfectly well.
M: Until fuel prices double. Then everybody will suddenly be very interested in the field down the road. My grandad lived through shortages, and he never trusted a lorry in his life.
W: That's a very long way off, if it ever happens at all.
M: Well, here's something even you might like. A scheme like this brings work into the area. Somebody has to run the plots, deliver the produce, sell it in the little shop on the corner.
W: Now that I can get behind. My friend's café started buying salad from a rooftop garden round the corner, and her lunchtime trade has doubled. The money stays in the neighbourhood instead of disappearing into some big company.
M: So you're coming round to the whole idea, then?
W: To the jobs, yes. Just don't ask me to dig anything.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Housing space is more important than farming space. → Woman. W: "Surely a roof over somebody's head comes before a row of carrots?"; M phản đối: "is it really one or the other?" + "Not every square metre has to become a block of flats." Bẫy: M "I'll grant you there's a shortage" (đồng ý một phần) rồi gạt đi.
2. Urban farming is appealing. → Man. M: "the whole idea excites me" + "I'd sign up tomorrow."; W phản đối: "It all sounds a bit twee to me." Bẫy: M đáp "Each to their own" – không phải đồng ý.
3. Cities need more food. → Man. M: "Sooner or later there won't be enough to go round unless we grow more of it ourselves."; W phản đối: "Oh, come on." + "The system copes perfectly well." Bẫy: không có 'food', phải hiểu "enough to go round".
4. Urban farming will benefit the urban economy. → Both. M: "A scheme like this brings work into the area."; W: "Now that I can get behind." + "The money stays in the neighbourhood". Bẫy: W vẫn nói "Just don't ask me to dig anything" – chỉ là đùa, không phủ nhận lợi ích kinh tế.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: About two years ago, in the spring of 2024, my cousin Linh dragged me along to the Imperial Citadel in Hue. She mainly needed somebody to carry her camera bag. I was not expecting much, since I had already seen photographs of it a hundred times. We arrived early in the morning, before the tour groups turned up. The whole place was silent apart from a gardener sweeping leaves near the main gate. The part I remember most clearly is Thai Hoa Palace, with its enormous red lacquered columns covered in gold dragons. Between old buildings and modern ones, I would choose the old ones almost every time. A new tower can be impressive for about ten minutes. An old building makes you curious. You start wondering who chose that doorway, why the roof is that shape, and what the room smelled like when it was full of people. I like the imperfection as well, the worn steps and the creaking floors. Modern buildings are more comfortable, and I would rather work in one. For the near future, I am planning a trip to Hoi An and My Son with my sister at the end of October, once the rain has eased. She has booked the tickets already. I want to see the Cham towers in particular. This time I have promised myself I will hire a proper guide, instead of wandering about reading the small signs and understanding nothing.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Last autumn I visited the Temple of Literature in Hanoi. I went there with my cousin on a Sunday morning. We arrived very early, so the place was quiet. The temple is more than nine hundred years old. I liked the old stone tablets with the names of students. An old man told us about the history for ten minutes. He said students walked for weeks to take the exams there. I took many photos of the red gates and the old trees. We stayed for about two hours and then had noodles nearby. I prefer old buildings to modern ones. A modern building looks nice, but it looks the same everywhere. An old building has a story, so I feel curious. I ask myself who lived there and how they worked. Old buildings are not comfortable, but they are interesting. Next month I will visit another old place. My sister and I will go to Hoi An for three days. We have already booked the train tickets. I want to see the old wooden houses near the river. We will also visit the old bridge at night. This time we will pay for a real guide. Last time I read the small signs and understood nothing.

groups.question: Why do you think sport brings people together?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: The match I always come back to is Vietnam against Thailand in the AFF Cup final. I watched it one December a few years ago at a coffee shop near my house. About thirty neighbours were squeezed onto plastic stools around one screen. My uncle had insisted we get there an hour early to claim a decent view. He was right, because by kick-off people were standing in the road outside. For the first half I was fairly relaxed. Once we scored, though, I was on my feet shouting with everybody else. The last fifteen minutes were honestly unbearable. I kept checking the clock, my heart was racing, and I could not sit still. When the whistle went, the street erupted. Somebody's grandmother was banging a saucepan, and half the city rode around with flags until midnight. Nobody in that street slept much that night. Looking back, what struck me was not the football. It was the fact that I was celebrating with people whose names I did not even know. I think sport brings people together because it is so simple. You do not need education, money or a shared background to understand who is winning. So a match creates an instant common language. It also gives people permission to show emotion in public, which many of us rarely do. And when a team represents a city or a country, supporting it becomes a small way of saying you belong somewhere.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: A few days before my birthday, Vietnam played Thailand in a big final. I watched the match in a small coffee shop near my house. About thirty neighbours sat there on plastic chairs. My father and I arrived one hour early for good seats. The owner put a big screen outside for everyone. In the first half I felt quite calm. Then our team scored, and everybody stood up and shouted. An old woman next to me hit a metal pot. The last ten minutes were very hard for me. My heart was beating fast and I could not sit down. When we won, people rode motorbikes with flags until midnight. I went out with them and shouted too. I think many people enjoy watching sport for simple reasons. First, you never know the result, so it is exciting until the last minute. Also, it is a cheap way to relax after work. You only need a screen and some friends. Finally, people like feeling part of a group. When your team wins, you share the happiness with thousands of other people. That is why my neighbours still meet at that coffee shop every weekend.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The match I always come back to is Vietnam against Thailand in the AFF Cup final. I watched it one December a few years ago at a coffee shop near my house. About thirty neighbours were squeezed onto plastic stools around one screen. My uncle had insisted we get there an hour early to claim a decent view. He was right, because by kick-off people were standing in the road outside. For the first half I was fairly relaxed. Once we scored, though, I was on my feet shouting with everybody else. The last fifteen minutes were honestly unbearable. I kept checking the clock, my heart was racing, and I could not sit still. When the whistle went, the street erupted. Somebody's grandmother was banging a saucepan, and half the city rode around with flags until midnight. Nobody in that street slept much that night. Looking back, what struck me was not the football. It was the fact that I was celebrating with people whose names I did not even know. I think people watch sport mainly because nobody knows how it will end. Films and novels are written in advance, but no one can tell you how a match will finish, and that uncertainty is addictive. Beyond that, it is an inexpensive escape: ninety minutes in which your own problems disappear. And it gives people a group to belong to, which matters more than we usually admit. My neighbours and I still meet at that same coffee shop, and the football is really just the excuse.

question_text: What do you think about children learning to ride a bicycle?
explanation: I think learning to ride a bicycle is very good for children. It teaches them balance and gives them confidence, because at first they are afraid of falling. It is also good exercise and it lets them play outside instead of sitting at home. Of course, parents worry about traffic, so children need a safe place to practise. In my opinion, every child should learn, and the earlier they start, the easier it is.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I think learning to ride a bicycle is very good for children. It teaches them balance and gives them confidence, because at first they are afraid of falling. It is also good exercise and it lets them play outside instead of sitting at home. Of course, parents worry about traffic, so children need a safe place to practise. In my opinion, every child should learn, and the earlier they start, the easier it is.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: It is one of the few skills you keep for life, so I would say it matters more than people think. The real lesson is not the cycling. It is the falling off, getting up and trying again while somebody watches, which children get fewer chances to do now. There is also freedom in it. A bike is the first way most children travel somewhere without an adult. The obvious worry is traffic, and in a city like Hanoi that worry is completely reasonable.

question_text: Why do fewer children play outside these days?
explanation: I think fewer children play outside now for several reasons. The main one is that they have phones and computers, so they can play games at home. Traffic is also much heavier than before, and parents do not feel safe letting children out alone. In many cities there are fewer parks and open spaces than there used to be. Children are also much busier with extra classes in the evening, so they simply have far less free time than before.

question_text: Mountain (Version 5)
options: A disturbing revelation
Our changing perspective towards mountains
A more intimate relationship
The wrong priority
Publicising one's achievements
A unique sense of achievement
A focus on sustainability
explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
1. Chọn "Our changing perspective towards mountains" vì đoạn văn so sánh xưa – nay: người ta từng nghĩ leo núi là thú chơi hẹp, nhưng có bằng chứng leo núi đã là môn thể thao nghiêm túc từ lâu; điều KHÁC biệt bây giờ là định nghĩa "chinh phục" = đứng trên đỉnh, tự mình nhìn xuống thay vì nhờ ảnh và lời kể của người khác.
2. Chọn "A unique sense of achievement" vì đoạn văn nói về cảm giác thành tựu sâu sắc (profound sense of accomplishment): hình dáng núi tượng trưng cho chinh phục, vượt nỗi sợ, đẩy giới hạn, cộng thêm adrenaline khiến người leo quay lại mãi.
3. Chọn "Publicising one's achievements" vì đoạn văn nói selfie trên đỉnh gần như bắt buộc — bằng chứng và cách để mọi người biết; sự thoả mãn riêng tư giờ được đăng, gắn giờ, chia sẻ (posted, timestamped and shared).
4. Chọn "The wrong priority" vì đoạn văn chỉ ra người leo tập trung vào bức ảnh hơn ngọn núi, coi hành trình chỉ là chướng ngại, bỏ qua cảnh báo → tai nạn; "personal image ends up mattering more than safety or responsibility" = đặt sai ưu tiên.
5. Chọn "A disturbing revelation" vì đoạn văn mở bằng kỳ vọng Everest vắng vẻ rồi lật lại "The reality is startling": ảnh "traffic jam" trên death zone, rác mỗi mùa, thử thách cá nhân thành cuộc đua thương mại. Bẫy: đoạn 4 cũng nói tai nạn nhưng không "hé lộ" sự thật gây sốc.
6. Chọn "A focus on sustainability" vì đoạn văn nói về cách vận hành expedition đổi theo hướng bảo vệ môi trường: giới hạn permit, đặt cọc trả lại khi mang rác xuống, clean-up climbs, "a mountain should be left cleaner than it was found".
7. Chọn "A more intimate relationship" vì đoạn văn kể Nan Shepherd đi "into the hills rather than up them", biết núi như biết một người bạn — "one visits a friend with no intention but to be with him".
👉 Mẹo: đọc câu đầu + câu cuối mỗi đoạn; các cặp dễ nhầm là đoạn 3/4 (đăng ảnh vs ưu tiên sai) và đoạn 4/5 (tai nạn vs sự thật gây sốc ở Everest).

extra_data.title: Mountain (Version 5)

paragraphs.text: It's often thought that mountaineering has never attracted much serious attention - a niche pursuit that only became popular once modern equipment made the peaks accessible. There is clear evidence, however, that people were treating climbing as a demanding sport long before the era of social media. What is different in modern times is that many people now define conquering a mountain as standing on its summit - the particular thrill of being on top of the very thing you have just overcome, with the whole landscape spread out below, rather than relying on the photographs and accounts that other climbers have provided.

Climbing a mountain often leads to a profound sense of accomplishment. Because of their very shape, rising steeply to a single point, mountains stand for conquest and struggle, and reaching the top of one carries that meaning with it. But there is more to it than that: it represents not just reaching a physical summit but also conquering personal fears and pushing one's limits, creating memories that last a lifetime. There is also the adrenaline rush that comes with it - the same surge of excitement that draws people to other adventure sports, and one reason why so many climbers return to the mountains long after they have proved whatever they set out to prove.

Reaching the summit is no longer enough on its own. Taking a selfie at the top has become almost obligatory - the proof that the climb actually happened, and the means by which everyone else gets to hear about it. What was once a private satisfaction is now something to be posted, timestamped and shared within hours of the descent. This turns personal milestones into public spectacles that can inspire others, though it also raises awkward questions about authenticity: whether the climb was made for its own sake, or for the picture at the end of it.

In recent years, some climbers have become more focused on the photograph than on the mountain itself. Only the summit seems to count, as if there were nothing beautiful about the journey up, as if the hours of effort and the shifting landscape were merely an obstacle between the climber and the picture. Warnings go unheeded because nobody wants to turn back empty-handed, and in some cases this obsession with online fame has led to serious accidents. Reaching a major peak now also demands complicated organisation - permits, guides, bottled oxygen, a support team booked months in advance - and all of this can detract from the enjoyment of the climb. Personal image ends up mattering more than safety or responsibility.

You might expect the world's highest mountain to be an empty place - so hostile, so far beyond ordinary human endurance that hardly anyone would set foot there. The reality is startling. Photographs from recent seasons show a "traffic jam" of climbers on Everest, queuing along a single fixed rope in the death zone, waiting hours for their turn at the top. When a weather window opens, the ascent effectively becomes a race between them, the other climbers and the weather itself. Meanwhile the slopes carry the waste of every season, and what was once a personal challenge has become a commercial race measured in photographs and fame rather than respect for the mountain.

The pressure on high-altitude environments has forced a change in how expeditions are run. Authorities in several climbing regions now issue only a limited number of permits each season, and operators are required to lodge a deposit that is returned only once they bring their rubbish back down with them. Some teams organise clean-up climbs, whose purpose is not the summit at all but the removal of equipment and waste abandoned by earlier parties. Behind these measures lies a shift in what counts as a successful trip: protecting the slopes now matters as much as standing on top of them, and a mountain should be left cleaner than it was found.

For most people a mountain is something to be conquered - a summit to be reached, a target to be ticked off. The Scottish writer Nan Shepherd saw it differently. She grew up within sight of the Cairngorms and spent a lifetime walking the same range, setting down what she found there in The Living Mountain. She went into the hills rather than up them, returning to the same corries and burns until she knew them the way one comes to know a person rather than a place: to be with the mountain as “one visits a friend with no intention but to be with him”.
